name: Vocabulary and Practice
title: Vocabulary and Practice
answer: This idea is that vocabulary practice for English learners and newcomers can be strengthened by technology, especially adaptive vocabulary tools and individualized listening and speaking software. It matters because students need repeated practice with the words their classes require, and one teacher cannot give every student that practice alone. The text also warns that short term vocabulary gains can fade without review over weeks and months.

sections.body: Vocabulary and practice is the part of English learner instruction where technology has the strongest evidence, according to the book. The idea covers adaptive vocabulary practice, individualized software for listening and speaking, and audio versions of texts that students can replay. It solves a practical problem: a teacher cannot provide unlimited practice time to each student, and newcomers need many encounters with academic words to recognize and use them. It also addresses the risk that vocabulary learned quickly may not stick. The response is to connect practice to class words and to plan review across weeks and months, not just days.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For vocabulary, tools such as Duolingo for Schools offer adaptive practice, and Duolingo allows younger students with automatic child protections, but the practice should connect to the words students need for their classes. Teachers should plan review of words over weeks and months, because short term gains can fade. For listening and speaking, individualized language practice software can add practice time that one teacher cannot provide to every student, while the teacher still teaches. Teachers can also use text to speech tools to create audio versions of texts at different speeds, or record their own, and students can listen as many times as they need. In the grade bands described, first graders used picture cards generated by AI for English as a foreign language, and middle school English learners used individualized language practice software in an urban district.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence label is that vocabulary is where the evidence for technology is strongest. It reports that meta analyses show large effects for technology assisted vocabulary learning across ages (Hao et al., 2021; Torres et al., 2025). In a small study with first graders learning English as a foreign language, picture cards generated by AI beat paper cards on a test at the end of the unit, but the advantage disappeared on a later test (Temiz, 2025). In a randomized trial with 221 middle school English learners in an urban district, students who used individualized language practice software gained more in oral and listening skills than students in the regular curriculum alone (Harper et al., 2021).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on what technology can do. Not every vocabulary gain lasts, and short term gains can fade without continued practice, so teachers should plan review over weeks and months. The teacher still taught, and the software extended the practice, which means the software does not replace instruction. Practice should connect to the words students need for their classes, so the choice of vocabulary stays with the teacher. Duolingo allows younger students with automatic child protections, but the decisions about which words to teach, how to review them, and how to use audio or software remain with the teacher.
